Memo: Multi-Mode, Resource-Constrained Scheduling Challenge

Overview
We are preparing the baseline schedule for a project composed of multiple interdependent activities that must share limited renewable resources and operate within a fixed financial cap. Each activity can be executed in one of several ways, each with distinct duration, resource draw, and cost. The scheduling challenge is to set start times and select execution modes so that all logical and timing requirements are met while finishing the overall project as early as possible and staying within budget.

Execution Modes and Tradeoffs
- Each activity must be delivered in exactly one execution mode.
- Faster modes shorten task durations but require more resources and/or higher cost; slower modes are more economical but extend task time.
- Mode selections drive both the time profile of the schedule and the spending plan, so the team must allocate acceleration where it creates the greatest schedule benefit for the least cost.

Dependencies and Timing Requirements
- Precedence relationships define which activities must finish before others can begin.
- Some dependencies include minimum delays (a successor must wait at least a specified amount of time after its predecessor finishes).
- Some dependencies also impose maximum delays (a successor must start within a specified time window after its predecessor finishes).
- In addition to inter-task links, some activities have earliest allowed start times (release dates) and others have hard deadlines by which they must be completed.

Resource Management and Safety Rule
- Resources are renewable: when an activity completes, the capacity it used is immediately returned to the pool.
- Activities cannot be interrupted once started; they run to completion in their chosen mode.
- Conservative safety rule for independent activities: if two activities are not linked by precedence and there exists even one pairing of their execution modes and one resource type for which their combined draw would exceed that resource’s capacity, then those two activities must not overlap in time. The schedule must explicitly sequence them—one must finish before the other starts. This rule is deliberately conservative: even if some mode combinations would fit concurrently, the potential for overload under any allowed mode pairing requires sequencing.
- Outside of this safety rule, there is no separate “at all times” capacity check. The pairwise sequencing decisions for potentially conflicting activity pairs are the sole mechanism we use to avoid resource overloads.

Budget Constraint
- The total cost of the selected execution modes is capped by the fixed project budget. This is a non-renewable constraint across the whole project and requires the team to prioritize where to invest in faster modes.

Scheduling Goal
Our aim is to choose a mode for every activity and sequence all work so that:
- All precedence links, minimum and maximum delays, release dates, and hard deadlines are respected,
- The pairwise resource safety rule is satisfied for all independent activity pairs,
- The total spend on selected modes does not exceed the budget,
- The overall project completion time (makespan) is minimized.

Implications for Planning
- Mode selection and sequencing are tightly coupled: expediting the right tasks can shorten the critical path, but may trigger more sequencing requirements under the resource safety rule.
- The presence of maximum delay constraints and hard deadlines limits how much we can defer work to relieve resource contention.
- The baseline schedule will explicitly document mode choices, the resulting order of activities (including enforced sequences among otherwise independent tasks), and the expected finish date under the budget cap.
